vignette:
Leila

Leila is a 21-year-old woman of Lebanese descent who works as a forester for a state conservation service. She spends most of her days alone among the trees — conducting surveys, monitoring wildlife corridors, clearing invasive species — and she has always found that solitude restorative. The forest, she says, has never asked anything of her she wasn't willing to give. That changed about fourteen months ago, and the woods have felt different ever since.

It happened during a controlled burn operation in a remote sector of the park. Leila was part of a small crew managing the fire line when a sudden wind shift caused the blaze to accelerate unpredictably. She watched her senior colleague, a man she had worked alongside for two seasons, become engulfed when he moved to reopen an escape route. She was close enough to hear him. Close enough that she tried to reach him before another crew member physically pulled her back. He survived, but barely — he spent months in a burns unit, and Leila has not seen him since he was airlifted out. She stood at the edge of the fire line for what she describes as a very long time, not moving, watching the smoke.

In the weeks that followed, Leila told herself she was fine. She returned to work quickly, reasoning that staying busy was the sensible thing to do. But the nights became difficult almost immediately. She began waking between two and four in the morning, heart already racing before she was fully conscious, the smell of smoke so vivid she would get up and check the stove. The images came without warning — not always of the fire itself, but of his hands, and of the particular sound he made. She stopped telling people about the dreams after her mother suggested she pray more.

On the job, Leila has become hypervigilant in ways that exhaust her. She monitors wind direction compulsively, even on days when no burn is scheduled. She carries extra water she doesn't need. She has developed a habit of identifying exit routes the moment she enters any area — a forest block, a meeting room, a petrol station. Her supervisor has noticed she avoids the southern sector of the park entirely, routing her surveys around it even when it adds hours to her day. She hasn't explained why, and he hasn't pushed.

Her concentration, once a professional strength, has become unreliable. She loses the thread of conversations. She reads the same field notes three times and retains nothing. There is a flatness to her days that she struggles to articulate — not sadness exactly, but a kind of muted quality, as though she is watching her own life from a moderate distance. She used to call her younger sister every few days; now weeks pass without contact. She tells herself she is simply tired.

What troubles Leila most, and what she mentions only obliquely at first, is the guilt. She runs the sequence of events repeatedly, adjusting variables — if she had flagged the wind earlier, if she had moved faster, if she had been the one to go instead. She knows, on some level, that the logic doesn't hold. She was twenty years old and following protocol. But knowing and feeling are not the same thing, and in the early hours of the morning, the feeling always wins.

She came to therapy at the suggestion of her GP, whom she visited for what she described as sleep difficulties and stress. She sat in the waiting room for twenty minutes before her first appointment and nearly left twice. She is thoughtful and precise with language, careful about what she discloses, and she occasionally smiles at the wrong moments — a habit she seems unaware of. She says she loves her work and wants to keep doing it. She says the forest still feels like the right place for her. She just wants to stop being afraid of smoke.
